Bagchi A.lab_name: Bagchi Lab, Cancer Genome and Epigenetics Program, Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute (La Jolla, California, USA)
Bagchi A.role: Cancer geneticist and associate professor at Sanford Burnham Prebys who uses chromosome engineering to find cancer genes, known for showing that MYC-amplified cancers depend on the neighbouring gene PVT1
Bagchi A.sub: Associate Professor, Cancer Genome and Epigenetics Program, Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute, La Jolla · University of Minnesota, Department of Genetics, Cell Biology and Development and Masonic Cancer Center (2014–2017) · Postdoctoral training, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, Alea Mills lab · PhD, Jawaharlal Nehru University, New Delhi
story: MYC is one of the most important cancer genes, and many tumours carry extra copies of it. Next to MYC on chromosome 8 sits PVT1, a gene long thought to make only non-coding RNA. The 2026 Genes and Development study found that a circular RNA made from PVT1 (circPVT1) actually carries the code for a tiny protein, which the team named Firefox (FFX). Firefox boosts AKT-mTORC1 signalling and cap-dependent translation, the main way cells make proteins, and this keeps MYC protein levels high. When Firefox was removed, MYC levels fell and MYC-amplified tumours grew less in mice carrying human cancer cells (xenografts). It points to an mTORC1-linked weak spot in MYC-driven cancers, shown in cells and mouse models.

Anindya Bagchi is the senior author, the scientist who led the work. The paper builds on a question Bagchi's lab has followed for more than a decade: why does PVT1 travel with MYC? In 2014, from the University of Minnesota, Bagchi's group showed in Nature that cancers with extra copies of MYC also gain PVT1 and need it, because PVT1 keeps MYC protein stable. A 2016 paper showed MYC and PVT1 working together in breast cancer.

Bagchi earned a PhD at Jawaharlal Nehru University in New Delhi and then trained as a postdoctoral fellow at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory in New York with Alea Mills. As first author of a 2007 Cell paper, Bagchi used chromosome engineering in mice, adding or deleting a large stretch of DNA matching human chromosome region 1p36, to identify the chromatin regulator CHD5 as a tumour suppressor that works through the p53 pathway.

Bagchi is now an associate professor in the Cancer Genome and Epigenetics Program at Sanford Burnham Prebys in La Jolla, part of its NCI-designated cancer center. The lab continues to engineer large genome rearrangements to find cancer genes and has discovered small proteins hidden in RNAs thought to be non-coding, including Firefox and, in a companion 2026 paper, Honeybadger, which restrains RAS-MAPK signalling. Bagchi also collaborates on brain tumour and pancreatic cancer studies at the institute.
Bagchi A.note: Title (Associate Professor), program, PhD (JNU New Delhi) and CSHL postdoc confirmed on the official SBP page; years of PhD/postdoc not given there. Start year at SBP still inferred from papers, so removed from sub.

Gailus-Durner V.lab_name: German Mouse Clinic, Institute of Experimental Genetics, Helmholtz Munich (Neuherberg, Germany)
Gailus-Durner V.role: Biochemist who co-founded the German Mouse Clinic at Helmholtz Munich and leads it as scientific head, running standardised testing of mouse models across many organ systems
Gailus-Durner V.sub: Scientific Head, German Mouse Clinic, Institute of Experimental Genetics, Helmholtz Munich (co-founded 2000–2001) · Senior scientist in bioinformatics, GSF Institute of Mammalian Genetics (1998) · Postdoctoral fellow, Waksman Institute, Rutgers University · PhD in biochemistry, University of Konstanz (1994)
story: Valérie Gailus-Durner is a co-author on two Atlas studies that relied on large-scale mouse phenotyping, the systematic measuring of many body functions in the same animals. EIS2016 showed that oral spermidine, a natural compound also found in food, lengthened the lives of mice, kept heart muscle from thickening and kept the heart able to relax normally between beats. The benefit disappeared in mice whose heart muscle cells lack the autophagy gene Atg5, so autophagy, the cell's self-cleaning system, was needed for the effect. The paper also included a human diet survey linking spermidine intake to lower blood pressure and fewer heart problems, but that part is observational and cannot show cause. NEF2013 gave rapamycin, the drug that blocks mTOR, to young and old mice and measured a very wide panel of body functions. Rapamycin lengthened life but changed only a few of the classic signs of ageing, so a longer life did not mean that ageing slowed down across the whole body. Both are mouse studies.

Gailus-Durner studied biology and earned a PhD in biochemistry at the University of Konstanz in Germany in 1994. Gailus-Durner then worked as a postdoctoral fellow at the Waksman Institute of Rutgers University in the USA on the genetics and gene regulation of meiosis, the cell division that makes eggs and sperm. In 1998 Gailus-Durner moved into bioinformatics at the GSF Institute of Mammalian Genetics, and in 2000 joined the Institute of Experimental Genetics led by Martin Hrabě de Angelis, where Gailus-Durner and Helmut Fuchs co-founded the German Mouse Clinic.

Gailus-Durner has been its scientific head since 2001, with main interests in metabolic diseases, rare diseases and ageing, as well as large-scale data analysis and quality management. Gailus-Durner appears together with Helmut Fuchs and the institute director Martin Hrabě de Angelis on more than a hundred PubMed papers. The German Mouse Clinic at Helmholtz Munich tests mouse models in a standardised way across many organ systems; its recent papers cover heart size, movement, behaviour, metabolism and blood values. Recent examples are a 2026 study of how heart weight should be compared between mice of different sizes, using data from more than 25,000 animals, and a 2026 mouse model of KMT2B-related dystonia, a genetic movement disorder. Gailus-Durner has also served on the executive board of the European EUMODIC project and sits on the steering committee of the International Mouse Phenotyping Consortium.
Gailus-Durner V.note: Official Helmholtz Munich page confirms title (Scientific Head of the German Mouse Clinic since 2001) and career. Name on that page: "Dr. Valérie Gailus-Durner" (kept).

Knopf BA.lab_name: Lamming Lab, Department of Medicine, University of Wisconsin-Madison (Madison, Wisconsin, USA)
Knopf BA.role: Graduate student in Dudley Lamming's lab at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and first author of a 2026 review that sets out the hallmarks of protein and amino acid restriction in aging
Knopf BA.sub: Graduate student, Cellular and Molecular Biology program, University of Wisconsin-Madison (Lamming lab, Department of Medicine and William S. Middleton Memorial Veterans Hospital, papers from 2025) · BS in Cell and Developmental Biology, University of Iowa
story: Bailey Knopf was first author of a 2026 review in Cell Press Blue (KNO2026) that asks what eating less protein does to an aging body. Across many organisms, cutting dietary protein, or only certain essential amino acids such as methionine, isoleucine and valine, improves metabolic health and can lengthen healthy life and lifespan. The review argues that the make-up of the protein, which amino acids it contains, matters as much as the amount, and that much of the effect runs through nutrient-sensing pathways, including mTORC1, the growth-control complex. Most of the evidence it summarises comes from animals.

Knopf is also a co-author of the Lamming lab's 2026 study on restricting single branched-chain amino acids in Alzheimer's model mice (BAB2025), in which cutting isoleucine or valine, but not leucine, improved metabolic health. PubMed lists about a dozen papers with Knopf's name since 2025, all from Lamming's group, including a 2025 preprint showing that the body's production of ketone bodies is not needed for the metabolic changes caused by calorie restriction in mice. Knopf studied cell and developmental biology at the University of Iowa (BS) and is now a graduate student in the Cellular and Molecular Biology program at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, doing doctoral research in the Lamming lab.
Knopf BA.note: Lamming lab members page lists Knopf as Graduate Student, Cellular and Molecular Biology, with BS from University of Iowa.

Javors MA.lab_name: Biological Psychiatry Analytical Laboratory, Department of Psychiatry, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Javors MA.role: Pharmacologist and professor at UT Health San Antonio who directs an analytical laboratory for biochemical and drug measurements, and a co-author of rapamycin studies in mice and in older people
Javors MA.sub: Professor, Departments of Psychiatry and Pharmacology, and Director, Biological Psychiatry Analytical Laboratory, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio · Adjunct Professor, College of Pharmacy, University of Texas at Austin · PhD in pharmacology, University of Colorado at Boulder (1979)
story: A drug can only be judged if you know how much of it actually reaches the blood. Martin Javors appears as a co-author on rapamycin studies from San Antonio, where the measurement of drug levels is part of the work. In the Atlas pilot trial KRA2018, 25 healthy adults aged 70 to 95 took daily rapamycin or placebo for at least eight weeks. The drug was well tolerated, with only small changes in red blood cells and no rise in blood glucose or insulin resistance over that short period. The trial was small and short and only checked safety, but it laid groundwork for larger human studies.

Javors is also a co-author of the Atlas study STR2022 from the NIA Interventions Testing Program, which tests possible anti-aging drugs in genetically mixed mice at three sites. Rapamycin plus acarbose, a drug that slows sugar uptake from the gut, started at nine months of age gave male mice a longer lifespan than rapamycin alone had given in earlier groups. In females the combination did about as well as rapamycin alone.

PubMed lists 16 papers with Javors that involve rapamycin, including earlier Interventions Testing Program reports such as the 2016 study in which metformin plus rapamycin extended mouse lifespan, and a 2015 study in which rapamycin shortened life in db/db mice, a model of type 2 diabetes. Most give the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio as the address.

Javors earned a degree in pharmacy at the University of Texas at Austin and a PhD in pharmacology at the University of Colorado at Boulder in 1979, followed by a pharmacology internship at the UT Health Science Center at San Antonio. Javors is a tenured professor in the Departments of Psychiatry and Pharmacology there and directs the Biological Psychiatry Analytical Laboratory, which makes biochemical measurements for psychiatric research, including tests for psychiatric drugs. Javors' own research has covered biochemical markers of alcohol and nicotine use, the brain messengers serotonin, dopamine and noradrenaline and their transporters, and how serotonin function relates to impulsivity.
sources: PubMed: Javors MA[Author] AND (rapamycin OR sirolimus) (16 records)

Al-Saadi RS.lab_name: Phillips Lab, Institute of Ecology and Evolution, University of Oregon (Eugene, Oregon, USA)
Al-Saadi RS.role: Doctoral student in Patrick Phillips' lab at the University of Oregon who studies how ageing differs between the sexes, using male C. elegans
Al-Saadi RS.sub: Doctoral student, Institute of Ecology and Evolution, University of Oregon (Patrick Phillips lab, papers 2025–2026) · Department of Biology, Syracuse University (Sarah Hall lab, 2026 paper)
story: Rose Al-Saadi is first author of ALS2026, a study in the tiny roundworm C. elegans. Most worm ageing research uses hermaphrodites, which make both eggs and sperm; this study looked at males. The team used a chemical switch (auxin-inducible degradation) to destroy DAF-2, the worm's insulin/IGF-1 receptor, throughout the body of adult males. Median lifespan rose by more than 440 percent, one of the largest lifespan gains reported for a single intervention, and the males stayed able to mate much later in life. Destroying DAF-2 only in the male germline, in contrast, shortened life, the opposite of what happens in hermaphrodites.

The insulin/IGF-1 pathway and mTOR are linked growth signals that both control ageing, so the paper shows that the sexes can respond differently to the same anti-ageing switch. The results are in worms and need testing in other animals.

Al-Saadi works with Patrick Phillips at the Institute of Ecology and Evolution of the University of Oregon on sex differences in ageing. A 2026 GeroScience paper from the pair tested seven compounds known to extend hermaphrodite lifespan: all lengthened male life, but only sulforaphane and metformin also kept males reproductively fit late in life. Earlier work in Sarah Hall's lab at Syracuse University, published in 2026, showed that a male worm's developmental history, including passage through the stress-resistant dauer stage, shapes how often worms cross-mate. The University of Oregon's Institute of Ecology and Evolution lists Al-Saadi as a doctoral student in the Phillips lab.
Al-Saadi RS.note: UO Institute of Ecology and Evolution graduate directory lists Rose Al-Saadi as doctoral student, Phillips lab. Role at Syracuse (degree there?) still not confirmed. ALS2026 has a bioRxiv preprint version (PMID 41278961).

Sparta B.lab_name: Deeds Lab, University of California, Los Angeles (Los Angeles, California, USA)
Sparta B.role: Quantitative cell biologist who trained in John Albeck's lab at UC Davis, where live single-cell imaging showed that the mTORC1-TFEB signalling axis tracks nutrients and growth factors continuously, and then moved to UCLA as a postdoctoral fellow
Sparta B.sub: Postdoctoral fellow, Eric Deeds lab, University of California, Los Angeles (IRACDA program, 2021 cohort) · PhD, University of California, Davis (John Albeck lab, papers 2015–2023) · BS in Biochemistry, Northeastern University
story: Breanne Sparta was first author of a 2023 eLife paper in this Atlas (SPA2023). Most experiments on mTORC1, the growth-control complex, grind up millions of cells and measure an average at a few time points. This study filmed single living human breast epithelial cells (MCF10A) carrying fluorescent reporters, and followed TFEB, a regulator of lysosomes and autophagy that mTORC1 holds outside the nucleus, together with AMPK and AKT activity. mTORC1-TFEB signalling adjusted smoothly to amino acids and insulin whether they were given alone, one after the other or together. At normal body levels of amino acids the three signals rose and fell in step, and these graded changes tracked how fast the cells were making protein. The results come from one cultured cell line.

Sparta studied biochemistry at Northeastern University (BS) and earned a PhD at the University of California, Davis, in John Albeck's lab, with a thesis on how growth and metabolism are coordinated in single living cells. That work also used live-cell reporters. As first author of a 2015 Journal of Biological Chemistry paper, Sparta showed that pulses of ERK activity triggered by the growth factor EGF depend on mechanisms at the receptor. Sparta co-authored a 2017 methods chapter on imaging ERK signalling with fluorescent biosensors, a 2017 modelling study of oscillations in MAPK signalling, and a 2021 Cell Metabolism paper on how single cells pass through temporary phases of resistance to drugs that block mitochondrial energy production.

Sparta then joined Eric Deeds' lab at the University of California, Los Angeles, as a postdoctoral fellow in the IRACDA program (2021 cohort). The research there asks how gene expression varies between cells in multicellular organisms.
